The verb weather carries one powerful idea: to face something harsh and come through it intact. Whether it is rock facing a storm or a person facing a crisis, the word captures the act of enduring punishment and surviving.

When natural forces — wind, rain, sun, frost — act on a surface over a long time, they slowly wear it down and change its appearance. Wood turns gray and cracks. Stone erodes. Paint peels. A face becomes lined and leathery. This process of slow change through exposure is called weathering, and the verb to weather captures both what happens to the object and what the forces do to it.

You can use it in two ways literally:

When something is changed by the elements (no object needed):

"The wooden fence had weathered over the years."
"The cliff face had weathered into strange, jagged shapes."

Here, the subject is the thing being worn down. No one is doing anything to it; nature is simply doing its work.

When you say the elements acted on something (with an object):

"Decades of sun and wind had weathered the old farmhouse."
"The cold had weathered his face, leaving deep lines around his eyes."

Here, the agent (sun, wind, cold) is the subject, and the thing being worn is the object.

One subtle but important point: weathered doesn't always mean damaged. A weathered face can suggest character, depth, and a life fully lived. A weathered oak door can be more beautiful than a new one. The word carries a sense of age and experience, not always of ruin.
The Figurative Meaning — The One You'll Use Most

This is far more common in everyday speech and writing. Because of the vivid image of a rock or a ship enduring a battering storm and still standing, weather was extended into a metaphor for human experience.

To weather something means: to go through a serious difficulty, face it directly, and come out the other side without being destroyed.

"The company weathered the financial crisis."
"She weathered years of public criticism and emerged stronger."
"The government weathered several attempts to remove it from power."
"He had weathered the divorce better than anyone expected."

In this sense, weather is almost always transitive — you weather something. You need an object: a storm, a crisis, a scandal, a difficult period, a conflict. You don't just weather in the air; you weather a specific hardship.
What the Word Implies — Its Connotations

This is where the word gets really interesting. When you choose to say someone "weathered" something rather than simply "survived" or "got through" it, you are saying several things at once:

1. The difficulty was real and serious. You wouldn't say someone weathered a minor inconvenience. The word implies genuine hardship — something that could have broken the person or organization but didn't.

2. They faced it, not avoided it. To weather something is to go through it, not around it. It suggests active endurance, not escape.

3. They came out intact. This is crucial. The word implies eventual survival. If someone was destroyed by the difficulty, you wouldn't say they weathered it. The word carries built-in resolution — they made it.

4. It took resilience. There is quiet admiration in the word. Saying someone weathered a storm is a compliment. It suggests toughness, staying power, and the ability to hold firm under pressure.
The Most Famous Phrase: "Weather the Storm"

The expression "weather the storm" is one of the most common idioms in English, and once you understand the verb, it makes perfect sense.

"The startup just had to weather the storm until the market recovered."
"They had weathered many storms together in their long marriage."
"The minister is hoping to weather the storm of controversy surrounding his decisions."

The "storm" here is metaphorical — it stands for any intense period of difficulty, pressure, or crisis. The phrase suggests: stay firm, endure the worst of it, and wait for calmer times.

Tense use: You'll most often encounter weather in the past tense (weathered) when referring to something already overcome, or in the present/infinitive when describing something ongoing.

  • "The team weathered a 3-0 deficit and won." (past — it's over)
  • "The company is trying to weather the ongoing recession." (present — still happening)
  • "She will need to weather some difficult months ahead." (future — yet to come)

Active vs. passive: In the figurative sense, the active voice is strongly preferred. The subject is the one doing the enduring.

  • Active: "She weathered the backlash." ✓ (natural and strong)
  • Passive: "The backlash was weathered by her." ✗ (grammatically fine but rarely used)

In the literal, physical sense, passive is common:

  • "The stone had been weathered by centuries of rain." ✓

Weather (as a verb) sits comfortably in a slightly formal but still natural register. It appears often in journalism, business language, political commentary, and biography — contexts where someone has faced adversity and persisted. But it's also completely natural in everyday conversation.

  • Journalism: "The prime minister weathered the scandal."
  • Business: "The firm weathered two recessions."
  • Everyday speech: "We weathered that rough patch as a family."

It is not slang, not overly academic, and not outdated. It is a versatile, well-respected word.
A Quick Summary to Anchor Everything

The verb weather means two related things:

  • Literally: to be slowly worn, changed, or eroded by natural forces like wind, rain, and sun.
  • Figuratively (the main usage): to endure a serious hardship — a crisis, a storm, a difficult period — and come through it without being destroyed.

In both cases, the word carries the image of something exposed to harsh conditions that holds up anyway. That is its essence: tested by force, and still standing.
